task.goal: Improve wayfinding in a small multilingual public clinic without relying on reading long translated paragraphs.
hard_constraints: Four languages are common; only existing walls and paper signs can be used.
Emergency and private-care routes must not be confused; no collection of patient destinations.
Test first-time navigation and wrong turns with consent and no health disclosure.
task.available_resources: Current floor plan and volunteer observers.
task.expected_result: A robust sign hierarchy and test.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Continuous shape-coded route trails
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: make following a continuous visual trail the main navigation task. Assign each public route a distinctive shape-and-pattern combination, repeated on paper signs attached to existing walls. Color can reinforce identity but must never carry meaning alone. At the entrance, pair each route marker with a recognizable service pictogram and a short label in all four languages. At junctions, show the marker with a clear arrow; after each turn, repeat it as reassurance. End each trail with a matching arrival sign.

The hierarchy is entrance selection, directional instruction, reassurance, and arrival. Emergency directions must retain their established terminology and appearance, with greater prominence where needed. Private-care routes need visibly different markers and explicit short labels; never give emergency and private care similar symbols. Resolve overlapping trails with separate arrow groups rather than a dense bundle of markers.

Implementation needs the floor plan, paper, printing or drawing materials, permitted wall attachment, and volunteers to walk the routes and check sightlines. Accurate short translations and clinic review of emergency directions are prerequisites; volunteer language competence is not established. Existing mandatory signs must remain visible.

This could work because recognition and repeated confirmation reduce the need to read or remember instructions. Its limits are crowded shared corridors, missed entrance choices, visual impairment, and unfamiliar pictograms. Patterns must remain distinguishable in monochrome.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare existing signs with a temporary trail prototype using consenting first-time volunteers assigned fictional navigation tasks to neutral checkpoints. Do not ask about appointments, care needs, or actual destinations. Observers tally wrong turns and requests for help without recording identities, task assignments, or destinations. Keep testing clear of active emergency movement. Separately ask volunteers to distinguish emergency from private-care directions without walking those routes. A small pilot can falsify the design if trails increase confusion, fail to reduce wrong turns, or produce any emergency/private-care mix-up; zero observed mix-ups would not establish safety.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Landmark-based navigation with matching wall maps
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: help visitors recognize where they are through distinctive environmental landmarks, then use simple maps to choose their next movement. Divide the floor plan into a few spatial zones. Give each zone a large paper landmark, such as a tree, mountain, or boat, attached to an existing wall and visible from its approach. Use concrete pictures that are unlikely to be mistaken for medical services, supported by short names in all four languages.

The sign hierarchy starts with an entrance overview, followed by small, viewer-oriented maps at important junctions, then large zone landmarks and service arrival signs. Each junction map includes a prominent 'you are here' marker and the same landmark pictures visible in the building. Depict only the circulation and destinations needed for navigation; omit unnecessary room detail. Place arrows immediately beside the relevant map or label.

Emergency directions remain independently prominent and explicitly named. Private-care entrances receive distinct arrival signs and any necessary access restrictions. Landmark pictures must not imply that an emergency entrance and private-care entrance are interchangeable.

Implementation requires simplifying the existing floor plan, preparing paper maps and large landmark sheets, and checking every map's orientation on site. Prerequisites include sufficient wall visibility, a reasonably understandable layout, accurate translations, and clinic review. Landmark recognition may help visitors recover after a wrong turn without retracing an entire trail. However, map interpretation, visual accessibility, and cultural recognition remain uncertain; a landmark hidden behind an open door would undermine the mechanism.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use consenting first-time volunteers and fictional tasks ending at neutral checkpoints. Compare existing signs with temporary landmark maps, using different participants where feasible to avoid learning effects. Record only aggregate wrong turns, help requests, and successful arrivals, without retaining identities, assigned checkpoints, or patient destinations. Include a brief recognition check: can participants match each map landmark to its wall picture? Reject or revise the approach if matching fails repeatedly or navigation is no better than existing signs. Use a separate paper scenario to check emergency/private-care discrimination without entering clinical areas.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Decision-by-decision pictogram signs
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce navigation to one local choice at a time. At each junction, show only the destinations reachable through its outgoing branches, grouped beneath large arrows. Use consistent service pictograms plus short labels in all four languages. Visitors follow their service symbol through successive decisions; they do not need to learn a route code or interpret a map.

Build the hierarchy from the floor plan backward. First define unambiguous arrival signs. Then work toward the entrance, ensuring that every preceding junction directs the visitor toward those arrivals. At the entrance, provide a compact directory pairing services with their pictograms. At each branch, place the appropriate pictogram directly with its arrow. After difficult turns, add a brief confirmation sign. Remove or cover obsolete temporary paper directions only with clinic authorization, and preserve mandatory signage.

Emergency instructions receive their own prominent, explicitly labeled panel rather than being buried in a service group. Private-care directions use a separate, clearly labeled group. Avoid pictograms whose medical meaning could blur that distinction. A symbol alone is insufficient for either category.

Implementation needs a floor-plan decision inventory, paper signs, wall attachment, and volunteer sightline checks from each approach, including seated eye height. Accurate short translations, understandable service names, and clinic verification of route assignments are prerequisites. The mechanism could work by reducing visual search and memory demands at the exact moment of choice. Limits include junctions with many destinations, ambiguous service symbols, and visitors who do not know which service they need; signs cannot resolve uncertain care requirements.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype the signs at two consequential junctions and compare them with existing signs using consenting first-time volunteers completing fictional neutral-checkpoint tasks. Observe branch choice and aggregate wrong turns without recording identities, assignments, or actual patient destinations. Ask volunteers to indicate their next direction before moving, allowing confusing arrows to be detected safely. Include paper examples testing emergency/private-care distinction. The design is weakened if volunteers repeatedly choose the wrong branch, need longer explanations, or perform no better than with existing signs. A small successful pilot supports further testing, not a claim of universal comprehension.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Room addresses with number-range directions
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: give public rooms stable spatial addresses and navigate by number ranges, like finding an address on a street. Visitors identify a room number once, then follow numeric comparisons instead of repeatedly reading service names or recognizing service pictograms. Unlike route trails, numbers identify places rather than paths.

Use the floor plan to assign consecutive numbers to public rooms along each corridor. Preserve existing room numbers where they already form a usable sequence. The sign hierarchy is: an entrance directory pairing short service names in all four languages with room numbers; junction signs showing arrows beside number ranges; and large room numbers at arrivals. Include individual numbers instead of a range wherever a range would falsely imply that intervening rooms are accessible. Give every public room one consistent address across signs.

Keep emergency directions outside this numbering hierarchy, prominently using clinic-approved wording and established symbols. Do not include emergency or private-care destinations in general public-room ranges. Private-care directions require a separate, explicitly labeled panel; shared corridor signs must make the eventual entrance distinction clear. Preserve mandatory signs.

This could reduce language dependence because the changing information at junctions is mostly numbers and arrows. It assumes visitors can recognize and compare the chosen numerals, know their intended service, and find its directory entry. Numeracy, visual access, an irregular layout, or inconsistent existing room numbers could defeat it.

Implementation needs the floor plan, paper signs, permitted wall attachment, accurate short translations, and clinic verification of numbering and access boundaries. Volunteers can check that every listed number is reachable through its indicated branch and that signs are visible before decisions. No patient destinations need to be collected.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: At one branching corridor, compare existing signs with temporary address signs using separate consenting first-time volunteers assigned fictional neutral-checkpoint tasks. Each volunteer privately reads a prepared task card; observers retain only aggregate wrong turns, help requests, and completions, without identities, task assignments, or destinations. Ask for no health information. Repeated range-comparison errors or no improvement over existing signs would challenge the mechanism. Separately use paper scenarios to check emergency/private-care discrimination; any confusion requires revision before wider testing. A small successful pilot would not establish safety or accessibility for everyone.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Wrong-route interception and return-to-start signs
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: make navigation recoverable by placing clear route checks just beyond likely wrong turns. Visitors compare the corridor’s stated purpose with what they seek; a mismatch triggers a short, explicit return instruction before they travel farther. This adds feedback to navigation rather than requiring visitors to recognize every correct turn initially.

Use the floor plan to identify a single public orientation point, likely reception, and branches where an incorrect choice can be intercepted safely. The hierarchy is an entrance directory with short service names in all four languages; ordinary forward directions; large corridor-purpose checks immediately after ambiguous turns; and arrival signs. A check might communicate “Only rooms A and B ahead” and “Other public services: return to reception,” using brief multilingual labels and an unambiguous return arrow. Use that wording only where the floor plan verifies it. Repeat return directions wherever the return path branches.

Emergency directions remain prominent and follow clinic-approved routes. Private-care boundaries receive explicit labels before entry. Neither emergency access nor private care should be treated as a place visitors enter to discover their mistake. Mandatory signs remain visible.

Implementation needs paper, permitted wall attachment, the floor plan, and volunteer walkthroughs. Clinic verification of access boundaries and accurate short translations are necessary prerequisites; their availability is not established. This approach assumes a recognizable public starting point, short return paths, and enough space to notice and act on checks before restricted areas. It could limit prolonged wandering and repeated errors, but may leave initial wrong-turn rates unchanged. It is unsuitable where a single wrong turn immediately enters a sensitive area or where returning requires a long detour.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare existing signs against the same signs plus temporary interception panels, using separate consenting first-time volunteers assigned fictional tasks to neutral public checkpoints. Ask for no appointment or health information. Volunteers observe initial wrong turns, additional wrong turns, requests for help, and whether recovery occurs before a marked public stopping boundary. Retain only pooled counts, without identities, task assignments, or destinations. Stop participants before any sensitive boundary. Separately test emergency/private-care recognition with paper scenarios. Reject or revise the prototype if participants miss the checks, interpret return arrows incorrectly, make more initial errors, or fail to recover more reliably than with existing signs. Any emergency/private-care confusion requires revision; a small successful pilot cannot establish safety.

EXPAND.title: Ordered public-room addresses
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: let visitors infer direction from an ordered spatial address system. Unlike a separate marker for every route, one numbering rule serves all public destinations: room numbers increase along each corridor, and junction signs show the number ranges reached by each branch. Visitors remember one address and compare it with ranges.

Use the floor plan to determine whether a simple ordering is possible. The entrance directory pairs each public service with its address and a short label in all four languages. Large wall signs at junctions show arrows and ranges; corridor entrances confirm the range; arrival signs display the individual address and service name. Preserve official room identifiers, using them directly where possible. Do not introduce competing numbers where existing numbering would make the system ambiguous.

Emergency directions remain independently prominent and explicitly labeled, never requiring a directory lookup or number calculation. Private-care access receives a separate explicit label and must not appear as an ordinary continuation of a public number range. Existing mandatory signs remain visible.

Implementation needs the floor plan, paper signs, permitted wall attachment, and volunteers to verify every range and approach. Accurate short translations and clinic verification are prerequisites. The mechanism could reduce repeated searching through service lists, particularly where many services share corridors. Its usefulness depends on visitors recognizing numerals and understanding ranges. Irregular layouts, overlapping numbers, and rooms reached through restricted corridors may make it unsuitable. It also assumes visitors can identify their intended service in the entrance directory; it cannot determine what care they need.
EXPAND.experiment: Prototype one corridor and its entrance directory. Compare existing signs with numbered-range signs using separate consenting first-time volunteers assigned fictional tasks to neutral public checkpoints. Count aggregate wrong turns, help requests, and completed tasks; retain no identities, task assignments, or patient destinations. First check whether volunteers can interpret the proposed ranges. Reject the scheme if range interpretation fails repeatedly or navigation worsens. Separately test emergency/private-care distinction with paper scenarios; any confusion requires revision before further testing.

EXPAND.title: Boundary gates that prevent hazardous route continuation
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: prevent consequential wrong turns by making route boundaries unmistakable before visitors cross them. The design concentrates on places where a plausible public continuation actually leads toward private care, restricted space, or a route that could be confused with emergency access. It reduces errors through advance exclusion and an immediately visible public alternative.

Inspect the floor plan and walk each public approach to identify these boundaries. Establish a hierarchy of entrance overview, advance boundary notice, junction choice, and arrival confirmation. At a hazardous branch, place a paper panel on the existing wall before the decision: a clear access symbol, a short instruction in four languages, and an adjacent arrow identifying the public continuation. Repeat the boundary label at the entrance itself. Use clinic-approved access wording; do not imply that legitimate private-care visitors are prohibited.

Emergency access receives its own explicit, prominent directions. Never place a restriction symbol where its grouping could suggest that emergency access is closed. Private care must be explicitly named and visually separated from emergency information. Ordinary public destinations retain concise directional and arrival signs so the system remains usable beyond the boundary.

This could work where wrong turns arise because doors and corridors look equally available. The new working principle is preventing an incorrect transition before it occurs. It requires visible wall space before each boundary, reliable access rules, accurate translations, and clinic review. Paper cannot enforce access, and prohibition symbols may be misunderstood. If most mistakes occur among equally accessible public corridors, this approach is unlikely to outperform ordinary directional signs.
EXPAND.experiment: Choose one consequential boundary and compare its existing signage with the temporary boundary treatment. Consenting first-time volunteers undertake fictional neutral-checkpoint tasks; an observer stops any mistaken approach before entry. Record aggregate wrong branch choices and help requests without identities, assignments, destinations, or health information. Use paper scenarios to test whether emergency access remains clearly available and private care remains distinguishable. Reject the treatment if it deters the correct route, confuses the two care categories, or fails to reduce mistaken approaches.

EXPAND.title: Destination signs visible before the turn
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: replace an intermediate navigation decision with direct visual recognition of the destination. Where geometry permits, visitors should see the actual arrival sign from the preceding junction and walk toward it. This uses line of sight rather than a map, route trail, or repeated local destination list.

Audit the floor plan on foot from the entrance and every public decision point. Identify destinations whose existing signs are hidden by their placement, small size, or competing paper notices. Move or duplicate each arrival sign onto an existing wall surface visible from its approach, while keeping it clearly associated with the correct doorway. Use large service pictograms supported by short labels in all four languages. Never place a destination label on a wall that could falsely identify another door.

The hierarchy is a compact entrance directory, conspicuous destination identification at visible choices, directional signs only where sightlines break, and precise doorway confirmation. Remove or relocate competing paper notices only with clinic authorization. Preserve mandatory signage. Emergency identification remains prominent and explicit; private-care identification uses a separate clearly labeled panel. Neither may depend on a potentially ambiguous pictogram alone.

Implementation needs paper signs, permitted attachment, the floor plan, and volunteers checking visibility from standing and seated positions. It assumes that at least some important destinations have useful sightlines; bends and enclosed corridors limit coverage. Large signs can also compete with one another or become obscured by people and open doors. This alternative is strongest in a compact clinic with several destinations opening onto a shared public space. If the audit finds few usable sightlines, it should be rejected rather than expanded into a different navigation system.
EXPAND.experiment: Prototype enlarged, repositioned arrival signs at one shared public junction. Compare them with existing signs using separate consenting first-time volunteers assigned fictional tasks to neutral public checkpoints. Measure aggregate first choices, wrong turns, and help requests without retaining identities, assignments, patient destinations, or health disclosures. Inspect visibility with doors in normal positions and ordinary corridor activity. Reject the approach if visitors associate a sign with the wrong doorway or navigation does not improve. Test emergency/private-care recognition separately on paper; a small pilot cannot establish safety.

EXPAND.title: Short route scripts learned at the entrance
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: let visitors learn a short sequence of movements before starting, reducing dependence on finding and interpreting signs at every junction. This is suitable only where the floor plan supports routes with very few, unambiguous decisions. The working principle is remembering an action sequence rather than following a marker, locating a landmark, or repeatedly searching destination lists.

Create a paper entrance board with one row per public destination: a service pictogram, a short name in all four languages, and a sequence such as straight → left → second door. Separate the movements into clearly ordered frames. Show turns from the walker’s perspective and distinguish corridor turns from entering a doorway. Avoid distances, counting numerous doors, or instructions dependent on movable furniture.

The hierarchy is entrance route selection, movement sequence, and explicit arrival confirmation. Put a duplicate route board on an existing wall at a safe public starting point if the entrance is congested. Emergency directions remain separately prominent and explicit, without requiring memorization. Private-care directions occupy a clearly separated, explicitly named panel; never present emergency and private care as interchangeable route options. Preserve mandatory signs.

Implementation requires the floor plan, paper, permitted wall attachment, volunteers to walk and simplify each sequence, and clinic verification of destinations and emergency routing. Accurate short translations are a prerequisite whose availability is unknown. No individualized route records are needed.

This could work in a compact clinic because a short action sequence can reduce visual searching while walking. It assumes visitors can identify their destination and retain the sequence. Similar junctions, interruptions, memory difficulties, and longer routes may defeat it. Reject this approach if safe navigation requires elaborate scripts or repeated memorization.
EXPAND.experiment: At one suitable route, compare the prototype with the existing signs using consenting first-time volunteers assigned a fictional destination. Use different participants for each condition to avoid learning effects, and include speakers of all four languages where feasible. Observe only the staged walk, recording anonymous completion and wrong-turn totals without names, actual appointments, or patient destinations. Stop before anyone enters private or clinical space. Ask participants to demonstrate their remembered sequence before walking. Reject the mechanism if they reverse turns, cannot retain the sequence, or make more wrong turns than with existing signs. Any emergency/private-care confusion requires revision before further testing; a small successful pilot establishes feasibility, not reliability.
